slides.heading: Caffeine 3 times a day, last dose 8 hours before bed. What did the sleep lab record?
Sleep looked the same
slides.body: Total sleep time, time to fall asleep and sleep stages did not differ between caffeine nights and placebo nights.

slides.heading: Who this describes
slides.body: Twenty healthy men aged 18 to 35 who already had 300 to 600 mg of caffeine a day. Not women, not older adults, not occasional drinkers.

slides.heading: One thing did change
slides.body: Sigma-band brain activity in non-REM sleep was lower on caffeine nights. The authors read it as withdrawal beginning 8 hours after the last dose.

slides.heading: How sure?
slides.body: A small trial. The text gives no effect sizes or confidence intervals, only that the differences were not statistically significant.

slides.heading: Check your own timing
slides.body: Set your wake time and your last coffee in the simulator to see whether you are inside the window this trial tested.

decks.caption: A double-blind crossover trial in twenty young men: caffeine three times a day, ending 8 hours before bed, did not change measured sleep structure compared with placebo. A small trial in men aged 18 to 35, with no effect sizes reported. Simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Weibel J, Lin YS, Landolt HP, et al. The impact of daily caffeine intake on nighttime sleep in young adult men. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):4668. doi:10.1038/s41598-021-84088-x. Licence: CC-BY.

slides.heading: Intervals are sold on fat loss. Thirty-six trials, graded, tell it differently.
What changed
slides.body: In adults, interval training reduced body fat percentage by 1.53 points and raised fat-free mass by 0.51 kg, compared with no exercise.

slides.heading: The grades run backwards
slides.body: Certainty for the lean-mass result: high. For body fat percentage: low. The claim that gets the attention has the weaker evidence.

slides.heading: And the strong one is fragile
slides.body: Remove a single trial and the lean-mass gain becomes 0.46 kg lost, with an interval from 1.38 kg lost to 0.44 kg gained.

slides.heading: Who this describes
slides.body: 1,130 adults in trials of 3 to 15 weeks, most of them inactive and overweight or obese.

slides.heading: What to hold loosely
slides.body: The trials disagreed with each other on body fat, and measured it with different tools.

slides.heading: Build the programme, see the evidence
slides.body: Pick a type of interval, burst length and rest in the simulator. Each choice shows its estimate and how far it can be trusted.

decks.caption: Thirty-six randomized trials of interval training in adults, pooled and graded. Body fat percentage fell by 1.53 points, at low certainty. Fat-free mass rose by 0.51 kg, at high certainty, though the result depends on one trial. Full read and simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Khodadadi F, Bagheri R, Negaresh R, et al. The Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training Type on Body Fat Percentage, Fat and Fat-Free Mass: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. J Clin Med. 2023;12(6):2291. doi:10.3390/jcm12062291. Licence: CC-BY.

slides.heading: 8,000 steps on 1 or 2 days a week. What happened over 10 years?
The headline number
slides.body: After adjustment, people with 1 to 2 such days had a 10-year risk of death 14.9 points lower than people with none.

slides.heading: More days added little
slides.body: At 3 to 7 days the gap was 16.5 points. The curve went flat at 3 to 4 days.

slides.heading: Who this describes
slides.body: 3,101 US adults aged 20 or older, tracked for 1 week, then traced through death records. Observational: nobody was assigned to walk.

slides.heading: The groups were not alike
slides.body: Mean age was 63.7 in the zero-day group and 46.0 in the 3-to-7-day group. Adjustment narrows that difference. It cannot erase it.

slides.heading: What this cannot show
slides.body: Steps were measured for 1 week only. People in poor health walk less, so part of the gap is illness, not walking.

slides.heading: Try the adjustment yourself
slides.body: Open the simulator to watch the gap change as each adjustment is added, then add the weekly target to your Life Game.

decks.caption: A 10-year follow-up of 3,101 US adults: reaching 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week was associated with a risk of death 14.9 points lower than never reaching it (95% CI 18.8 to 10.9). An observational study, and the groups differed in age and health. Source and simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Inoue K, Tsugawa Y, Mayeda ER, Ritz B. Association of Daily Step Patterns With Mortality in US Adults. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(3):e235174. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.5174. Licence: CC-BY.

slides.heading: 1 g of black pepper in a breakfast egg. What did blood glucose do?
Lower at 30 minutes
slides.body: After the pepper breakfast, blood glucose was lower than after the plain one at the 30-minute reading. Added up over 3 hours, the meals did not differ.

slides.heading: Who this describes
slides.body: 20 healthy adults in their early twenties, one breakfast per version. Nobody with diabetes took part.

slides.heading: Turmeric alone showed nothing
slides.body: 1 g of turmeric without pepper showed no glucose effect. The authors think the dose was too low.

slides.heading: How sure?
slides.body: A small trial of single meals. The text gives no effect sizes and no confidence intervals. The trial measured no hormones, so the mechanism is a proposal.

slides.heading: Compare the four breakfasts
slides.body: Pick a meal in the simulator to see what the trial recorded after it.

decks.caption: A crossover trial in 20 healthy young adults tested 1 g of black pepper in a breakfast egg. Blood glucose was lower at 30 minutes than after the plain meal. The 3-hour total did not differ, turmeric alone showed nothing, and the text gives no effect sizes. Simulator at the link in bio.
